title: Quiche Lorraine
subtitle: a French tart of bacon, cream, and egg in a crisp pastry case
excerpt: Quiche Lorraine is the original and best of the quiche family. The filling is nothing more than bacon, eggs, cream, and a little nutmeg -- it sets into a custardy, silky slice. No onion, no cheese in the custard (though a little gruyere on top is traditional).
sourceNotes: From the Lorraine region of north-eastern France. One of the most copied French dishes in British home cooking.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bake, cool, and refrigerate. Serve at room temperature or warmed at 150C for 15 minutes.

content.text: The custard should be poured in with the tart case already in the oven on the pulled-out shelf -- this avoids carrying a full tin across the kitchen. Pour slowly and fill to just below the pastry rim. The filling needs a low oven and patience; a wobbly centre when you take it out is correct.

items.prepNote: 1 yolk for pastry, 3 whole for filling

content.text: Make the pastry: rub butter into flour to fine crumbs. Add the egg yolk and 2 tbsp cold water. Bring together and chill 30 minutes.
Roll and line a 23cm tart tin. Blind bake at 200C for 15 minutes with beans, then 5 minutes without. Reduce oven to 180C.
Fry about 200g streaky bacon lardons in a dry pan until golden. Drain and scatter over the pastry base. Add grated gruyere if using.
Whisk the 3 eggs with the cream, milk, a good pinch of salt, and the nutmeg.
Place the tart tin on the oven shelf and pour in the custard. Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until just set with a very slight wobble in the centre. Cool for 20 minutes before slicing.

items.cause: Oven was too hot, or baked too long.
items.fix: A quiche needs a gentle oven -- 180C maximum. Remove it when the centre still wobbles slightly. It will set as it cools.

items.cause: Not blind baked for long enough, or custard was too wet.
items.fix: Brush the blind-baked case with a little beaten egg and return to the oven for 2 minutes to form a seal before adding the filling.

content.text: Quiche Lorraine comes from the region of Lorraine in north-eastern France, which was under German influence for long periods and whose food reflects both cultures. The dish was introduced to British cooking in the 1970s and became a staple of dinner party menus. It is now eaten across Britain as everyday food -- served warm, at room temperature, or cold from the fridge.
